audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: all three Tönjes 1910 quotations are verbatim in the text we hold at the stated pages. (2) The record is internally split: the 'tonal' kind rested on a publisher blurb and Wikipedia for Halme 2004, while the quoted passage is a 1910 missionary teaching grammar describing dynamic penult stress with stem-initial deviations. Open sources downloaded now (Halme 2006 p.160; Otten 2006 review §2, §7; Elderkin 2006) plus the already-held Hurskainen & Halme 2001 p.399 give first-hand/scholarly open-text confirmation that Kwanyama is analysed as a lexical+grammatical H/L tone language with rightward tone shift; none mentions stress, and nothing found contradicts the tonal coding (catalog precedent: Herero, Fipa coded the same way when an old missionary 'accent' statement sits under a modern tonal description). So the classification stands and its evidence can be upgraded from blurb/Wikipedia to

sources.citation: Halme, Riikka. 2006. Harmonic versus non-harmonic final vowel in the verbal inflection of Kwanyama. Studia Orientalia 103: 159-171.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: No stress statement. p.159: 'Now that the basics of the Kwanyama tonal system are known (Halme 2004)'; p.160: 'The lexical H(igh) or L(ow) tone of the verb is marked next to the gloss of the base. Tones shift in Kwanyama one mora to the right'. First-hand statement by the author of the reference tonal grammar.
sources.note: First-hand open statement by Halme of the lexical H/L tone system and rightward tone shift (p.160); citable primary confirmation of 'tonal'. downloaded now; silent on stress.

sources.citation: Otten, Dirk. 2006. [Review of] Halme, Riikka 2004. A Tonal Grammar of Kwanyama (Namibian African Studies 8). Afrikanistik-Aegyptologie-Online 2006. doi:10.18716/ojs/aaeo/2006_3514
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: No stress statement. Characterises Halme's analysis: Kwanyama applies rightward 'tone shift', 'high doubling' and 'floating low deletion' without exception; 'Die Opposition Hochton vs. Tiefton ist Halme zufolge ein inhaerentes Merkmal des Lexems' with minimal pairs (ila L 'go for' vs ila H 'fetch'); ~6,000-entry tone-marked lexicon; book is XII+299 pp with a short segmental-phonology overview before the tonal chapters.

sources.note: The modern systematic description on which the 'tonal' classification nominally rests was never opened; its segmental/prosodic preliminaries (ch. before the tone chapters, per Otten 2006 §4) would settle whether any penultimate or stem prominence (Tönjes's 1910 'Betonung' rule) is retained alongside H/L tone, i.e. whether the record should read 'tonal, no stress' or 'tonal with penult stress'.
